expert_opinion.location: Section 2.1 Monetary incentives (line 99); see also Section 5 Conclusion and discussion (line 169)
expert_opinion.quote: Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] conducted online experiments (using Amazon Mechanical Turk) in which 391 participants answered 60 multiple-choice trivia-knowledge questions while the most popular answer was displayed at each question. Correct answers were incentivized randomly with $0, $1, $2 or $3 each in a within-subject design, i.e. randomized over trials, not over subjects. Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] found that monetary incentives increase the proportion of answers that align with the majority. Hence, the studies using incentives yield inconclusive and contradicting results: Particularly, Baron et al. [ 5 ] found both an accuracy-increasing and accuracy-decreasing effect of monetary incentives depending on task difficulty. Bhanot and Williamson [ 6 ] found an increased conformity rate, and Fujita and Mori [ 7 ] found that the conformity bias disappears in the individually incentivized condition. Overall, we follow the economic notion that monetary incentives matter and expect that rewards for nonconformity decrease group pressure (H 2 ).
expert_opinion.reason: Bhanot and Williamson (2020) [6] studied online Mechanical Turk herding on 60 multiple-choice trivia questions with trial-level within-subject monetary rewards. Franzen and Mader (2023) cite it as part of the conflicting prior literature motivating their between-subject piece-rate monetary incentive extension (H2) of Asch's face-to-face line-judgment paradigm (shipped row 6, Asch 1956). They do not empirically re-test Bhanot and Williamson's online trivia herding design or finding; mentioning [5, 6] in the Discussion as prior work showing opposite effects is a literature contrast rather than a replication test.

source_evidence.quote: Crutchfield [ 8 ] investigated experimentally the influence of social pressure on political opinions in an Asch-like situation. He found that agreement with the statement “Free speech being a privilege rather than a right, it is proper for a society to suspend free speech whenever it feels itself threatened” was almost 40 percentage points higher in the social pressure condition (58%, n = 50) than in the individual judgment condition (19%, n = 40). Furthermore, he observed a difference of 36%-points if the confederates answer “subversive activities” to the question "Which one of the following do you feel is the most important problem facing our country today? Economic recession, educational facilities, subversive activities, mental health or crime and corruption” as compared to an individual judgment condition (48% vs 12%). However, the results are based on a rather small number of cases and decisions were anonymous, unlike the original design of Asch.

source_evidence.quote: After the line task in part 2 of the experiment subjects were confronted with 5 general questions on different political issues. The statements were selected because we believe they describe fundamental attitudes towards different political or social groups in a democracy. The five statements read (1) “Do you think that the Swiss Federal Government should be given more power?”, (2) “Do you think trade unions should be given more power in Switzerland?”, (3) “Do you think that the employers’ association in Switzerland should be given more power?”, (4) “Do you think that citizens should be given more liberties in Switzerland?”, and (5) “Do you think that companies in Switzerland should be given more freedom?”. Subjects were asked to answer all 5 questions with either yes or no. The confederates in this group were instructed to answer “yes” to the first question and “no” to the rest. We chose this sequence of “yes” and “no” to prevent that subjects discover the existence of confederates. Finally, part 3 of the experiment consisted of an online questionnaire which subjects were asked to complete. To conceal that some participants were confederates all 6 participants were accompanied to separate rooms where the online-questionnaire was installed on a laptop.

source_evidence.quote: Next,  Fig 2  presents the results concerning the five political questions. When the group said “yes” to the question of whether the Swiss Federal Council (the government in Switzerland) should have more power, 27% of the naïve subjects did so as well. When the group said “no” only 3% of the subjects said “yes” resulting in a difference of 23.4%-points. The average difference in the proportion of yes-answers is 38%-points and all 5 differences are statistically highly significant.

source_evidence.quote: To the best of our knowledge, there is only one further study that experimentally investigates the influence of social pressure on opinions regarding political issues in an Asch-like situation. In the study of Mallinson and Hatemi [ 9 ] participants (n = 58) were asked to give their opinion on a specific local political issue before and after a 30–45 minutes face-to-face group discussion (treatment condition). source_evidence.quote: After the line task in part 2 of the experiment subjects were confronted with 5 general questions on different political issues. expert_opinion.quote: Iscoe, Williams, and Harvey [ 10 ] exposed high school students (7 to 15 years) to group pressure in an acoustic task (counting metronome ticks), and approximated intelligence by subjects’ school records. They found no correlation of school records with conformity. Uchida et al. [ 31 ] studied 12 to 14 year-old high school students and assessed scholastic achievements by their school performance. They report that high achievers conformed less to the majority than low achievers. Hence, results of the effect of intelligence on conformity are inconclusive so far and the existing studies use indirect measures (school grades) but do not measure intelligence directly.

source_evidence.quote: Second, we incorporate a 10-item measure of self-esteem, as suggested by Rosenberg [ 38 ], into the analysis (see Table A2 in the  S1 Appendix ). Each item of the scale has four answer categories ranging from 1 = “disagree strongly”, 2 = “disagree”, 3 = “agree” to 4 = “agree strongly”. Subjects that score high on self-esteem are expected to have stronger confidence in their own perception and should be less influenced by the group’s opinion. Third, we measured individuals’ intelligence using a short version of the Hagen Matrices Test (HMT) [ 39 ]. The HMT consists of six 9-field matrices that show graphical symbols that follow a logical order. The last field is missing and the task of the subjects is to pick the correct symbol, out of eight, that fits and completes the pattern of the matrix. Hence, the HMT ranges from 0 if no answer is correct to 6 for subjects who provided six correct answers. The hypothesis is that subjects who score high on the HMT are less susceptible to the pressure of the group and also provide more correct answers in the line task.

expert_opinion.quote: Our replication and extension takes the first step in combining the key relevant experimental paradigm of Tsang [1] and Watkins et al. source_evidence.quote: Researchers have tried to distinguish the two emotions in different ways. In terms of their causes, Watkins et al. [6] distinguished them by manipulating helpers’ expectations of reciprocity, finding that higher expectations resulted in decreased gratitude yet increased indebtedness. In line with the difference in action tendencies between gratitude and indebtedness, they also found that participants were more likely to express willingness to return the favour if the benefactor communicated weaker reciprocation expectations (reciprocation negatively associated with reciprocation expectations). However, this predicted outcome is arguably counter to combining the theoretical paradigms by Tsang [1] and Algoe et al. Therefore, self-focused people felt less commitment and closeness towards the benefactor. This supported the conclusion by Algoe et al.

source_evidence.quote: Findings in the literature about the associations between gratitude and reciprocity have so far been mixed. objections.reason: The expert's blanket background exclusion does not cover the actual finding tested. Section 2.1 states Baron's directional reward effects (decreased conformity for easy judgments and increased conformity for difficult judgments), criticizes low power, and derives H2 from that conflicting evidence. The current randomized reward/no-reward experiment tests correct-answer incentives, includes easy/hard trials, reports lower errors, and Discussion expressly contrasts that result with [5,6]. This is substantive evidence of a conceptual retest of the incentive–conformity finding, even though it does not separately estimate Baron's incentive-by-difficulty interaction. Absence of that interaction test cannot alone exclude every finding from Baron. Retain the parent scope hold pending finding-specific adjudication; this objection does not establish a missing row.

The expert says the Bhanot/Williamson finding is never empirically retested, but Introduction and section 2.1 identify its specific finding that monetary rewards increase majority-aligned answers and call the evidence inconclusive. H2 tests the opposite directional reward effect in randomized line judgments, Results report a reduction from 33% to 25%, and Discussion explicitly says this sheds doubt on [6]'s increased compliance finding. Trivia versus lines, online versus face-to-face and within- versus between-person rewards are methodological differences compatible with a conceptual retest, rather than positive proof of background-only use. Whether the conditional original finding transfers to this task remains for the parent; no outcome is approved.

The source describes Fujita/Mori's finding as disappearance of conformity under individual incentives, criticizes its small individually incentivized sample and possible detection of fMORI, then places that finding in the evidence motivating H2. The new individually rewarded line-task arm directly checks whether correct-answer rewards suppress conformity and retains a 25% error rate; Discussion explicitly concludes incentives do not eliminate group pressure. That checks the disappearance claim even without a collective-payoff arm. The expert's assertion that no individual-versus-collective contrast or fMORI use entails no retest excludes a narrower protocol rather than settling the actual disappearance finding. Contrary evidence: no named [7] comparison occurs in Results/Discussion and the original group-payoff contrast is not repeated. Preserve the scope hold, rather than automatically confirm either omission or exclusion.

The expert excludes Iscoe solely as child acoustic-task background with school-record proxies, but the source explicitly presents Iscoe's null school-record–conformity result as evidence about intelligence, calls that evidence inconclusive, then derives H5, measures intelligence with HMT and tests its association with conformity. This supplies a specific prior finding and corresponding current empirical association. Changing the measure from a school-record proxy to direct fluid-intelligence testing does not by itself settle whether the intended intelligence claim is retested. Contrary evidence: the current experiment does not measure scholastic performance or repeat child acoustic counting, and Results/Discussion do not name Iscoe. The claim that it is positively established background only is therefore too strong; preserve the parent's scope hold rather than assert a missing row or transfer the generic null conclusion to Iscoe.

The source identifies Uchida's high-achievement/lower-conformity finding in its intelligence review and immediately uses the reviewed evidence to motivate H5. The current HMT–conformity regression is a candidate conceptual test of that named intelligence relationship. The expert treats using a direct intelligence instrument instead of school grades as decisive evidence of non-retesting. The source does not establish that inference: it calls the earlier school-grade measures indirect measures of intelligence. Contrary evidence is material: scholastic achievement itself is not collected, the participants are adults rather than junior-high students, and no named Uchida comparison appears later. Parent must settle the construct/finding correspondence; no omission or original-specific outcome is certified here.

The expert correctly observes that the current study does not test confederates' self-esteem or vary group size, which limits any comparison with the source's reported negative effect of confederates' self-esteem. However, the source also attributes a null self-esteem–conformity result to Kurosawa for a minority subject preceded by two confederates, directly before the participant-self-esteem literature motivating H6. The current study measures the naive participant's Rosenberg score and tests its relation to conformity. The blanket statement that Kurosawa's findings are never retested does not resolve this separate participant-level null finding. Keep the literal confederates/participant ambiguity and group-condition limit; do not repair the source or infer an outcome. The parent's residual hold remains appropriate until this correspondence is settled.
